equation_request.abstract: We investigate the influences of variables on a Boolean function $f$ based on the quantum Bernstein-Vazirani algorithm. A previous paper (Floess et al. in Math. Struct. in Comp. Science 23: 386, 2013) has proved that if a $n$-variable Boolean function $f(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})$ does not depend on an input variable $x_{i}$, using the Bernstein-Vazirani circuit to $f$ will always obtain an output $y$ that has a $0$ in the $i$th position. We generalize this result and show that after one time running the algorithm, the probability of getting a 1 in each position $i$ is equal to the dependence degree of $f$ on the variable $x_{i}$, i.e. the influence of $x_{i}$ on $f$. On this foundation, we give an approximation algorithm to evaluate the influence of any variable on a Boolean function. Next, as an application, we use it to study the Boolean functions with juntas, and construct probabilistic quantum algorithms to learn certain Boolean functions. Compared with the deterministic algorithms given by Floess et al., our probabilistic algorithms are faster.

specification.problem: Given oracle access to a Boolean function f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}, estimate the influence (dependence degree) Inf_i(f) of each input variable x_i on f using repeated runs of the Bernstein-Vazirani circuit, exploiting the claim that a single run outputs a string y whose i-th bit equals 1 with probability exactly Inf_i(f).
specification.reconstruction_scope: Scoped to the core claim and the resulting approximation algorithm: (1) the Bernstein-Vazirani circuit applied to a general (not necessarily linear) Boolean function f via a standard bit-flip oracle, (2) the output distribution over y and the identity Pr[y_i=1]=Inf_i(f), and (3) a sampling estimator for all n influences from T independent runs. A tiny explicit instance (n=2, f=x_1 x_2, i.e. AND) is given as an assumption. Outside scope: the paper's analysis of Boolean functions with juntas, the probabilistic quantum learning algorithms for specific function classes, their exact query counts, and the speed comparison with the deterministic algorithms of Floess et al.

equations.label: Bit-flip oracle for f
equations.description: Standard oracle model used by the Bernstein-Vazirani circuit; with the ancilla in |-\rangle the oracle acts as a phase kickback (-1)^{f(x)}.
equations.justification: The Bernstein-Vazirani circuit is conventionally defined with a bit-flip oracle and a |-\rangle ancilla; the abstract only names the circuit, so this is recalled background.
assumptions: f is given as a standard bit-flip oracle U_f; the abstract does not specify the oracle model.

equations.label: Bernstein-Vazirani circuit state before measurement
equations.latex: (H^{\otimes n}\otimes I)\,U_f\,(H^{\otimes n}\otimes I)\,|0^n\rangle|-\rangle = \sum_{y\in\{0,1\}^n}\hat f(y)\,|y\rangle|-\rangle,\qquad \hat f(y)=\frac{1}{2^n}\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}(-1)^{f(x)\oplus x\cdot y}
equations.description: For an arbitrary Boolean function f, the Bernstein-Vazirani circuit produces a superposition over y with amplitudes equal to the Walsh-Hadamard (Fourier) coefficients of (-1)^f.
equations.justification: Follows exactly from applying H^{\otimes n}, phase kickback (eq_1), and H^{\otimes n} again; \sum_y \hat f(y)^2=1 by Parseval, so the state is normalized.
assumptions: Input register ordering: qubit j carries x_j and output bit y_j; x\cdot y is taken modulo 2.

equations.label: Output distribution and marginal of bit i equals influence
equations.description: Measuring the input register in the computational basis yields y with probability \hat f(y)^2; the probability that the i-th bit is 1 equals the influence of x_i. This is the paper's generalization of the Floess et al. result (if f does not depend on x_i, every \hat f(y) with y_i=1 vanishes, so y_i=0 always).
equations.abstract_quote: the probability of getting a 1 in each position $i$ is equal to the dependence degree of $f$ on the variable $x_{i}$, i.e. the influence of $x_{i}$ on $f$
equations.justification: The abstract states the probability of a 1 in position i equals the influence; the first equality is the Born rule applied to eq_2, and the identity \sum_{y_i=1}\hat f(y)^2=\mathrm{Inf}_i(f) is the standard Fourier formula for influence, consistent with the abstract's claim.
assumptions: Exact equality (not approximation) is claimed for a single run of the circuit.

equations.label: Influence (dependence degree) of a variable
equations.description: Combinatorial definition of the influence of x_i on f: the fraction of inputs at which flipping x_i changes f. It is 0 iff f does not depend on x_i and 1 iff f is odd in x_i.
equations.justification: The abstract calls this quantity the 'dependence degree' or 'influence' of x_i on f without defining it; this is the standard definition in Boolean function analysis and the one for which eq_3's Fourier identity holds.
assumptions: The paper's 'dependence degree' coincides with the standard influence; the abstract's 'i.e.' phrasing supports but does not prove this identification.

equations.label: Sampling estimator for all influences and sample bound
equations.description: Run the circuit T times, record the n-bit outputs, and estimate each influence by the frequency of 1s in position i; since y_i^{(t)} are i.i.d. Bernoulli(\mathrm{Inf}_i(f)) by eq_3, Hoeffding's inequality plus a union bound over the n positions gives additive accuracy \epsilon for all i simultaneously. The estimate is an approximation, not exact.
equations.abstract_quote: we give an approximation algorithm to evaluate the influence of any variable on a Boolean function
equations.justification: The abstract says an approximation algorithm is built 'on this foundation' (eq_3); the natural algorithm is frequency estimation from repeated runs. The specific estimator and Hoeffding/union bound are my reconstruction; the paper's actual sample-complexity statement is unknown.
assumptions: The paper's approximation algorithm is frequency estimation from independent circuit runs; the exact estimator and error analysis used in the paper are not given in the abstract.
Hoeffding bound and union bound are standard background, not paper evidence.

equations.label: Tiny explicit instance: n=2, f = AND
equations.latex: f(x_1,x_2)=x_1x_2:\quad \hat f(00)=\hat f(01)=\hat f(10)=\tfrac12,\ \hat f(11)=-\tfrac12,\qquad \Pr[y]=\tfrac14\ \forall y,\qquad \Pr[y_1=1]=\Pr[y_2=1]=\tfrac12=\mathrm{Inf}_1(f)=\mathrm{Inf}_2(f)
equations.description: Worked instance for circuit generation: 2 input qubits plus 1 ancilla, oracle is a Toffoli gate (target = ancilla). Each output bit is 1 with probability 1/2, matching the influence of each variable in AND (flipping x_i changes AND iff the other variable is 1).
equations.justification: No scope was supplied; this is the smallest nontrivial non-linear instance where influences are strictly between 0 and 1, so the identity in eq_3 is testable. Values computed directly from eq_2 and eq_4.
assumptions: Instance choice (n=2, AND) is my selection, not from the paper.
Oracle realized as a Toffoli gate with controls on the two input qubits and target on the ancilla.

registers.name: input
registers.role: holds x in superposition; measured at the end to give y, with y_i read from qubit i

registers.name: ancilla
registers.role: oracle target qubit prepared in |-\rangle for phase kickback; not measured (or measured and discarded)

specification.initial_state: |0\rangle^{\otimes n}_{\mathrm{in}}\otimes|1\rangle_{\mathrm{anc}} (the ancilla is then turned into |-\rangle by a Hadamard in step 1)

steps.description: Apply H to every qubit: the input register becomes the uniform superposition 2^{-n/2}\sum_x|x\rangle and the ancilla becomes |-\rangle.
Apply the oracle U_f once, which by phase kickback multiplies each branch |x\rangle by (-1)^{f(x)}.
Apply H^{\otimes n} to the input register, yielding \sum_y \hat f(y)|y\rangle on the input register with the ancilla left in |-\rangle.
Measure the input register in the computational basis to obtain y with probability \hat f(y)^2; bit y_i is 1 with probability exactly \mathrm{Inf}_i(f).
Repeat steps 1-4 independently T times (one oracle query per repetition), recording y^{(1)},\ldots,y^{(T)}, and form the frequency estimates of all n influences.

specification.measurement: Computational-basis measurement of the n input qubits after the final Hadamard layer; outcome string y with Pr[y]=\hat f(y)^2. The ancilla qubit is not needed and may be discarded.
specification.classical_postprocessing: For each i=1,\ldots,n compute \widetilde{\mathrm{Inf}}_i = (number of runs with y_i^{(t)}=1)/T. Choose T \ge \ln(2n/\delta)/(2\epsilon^2) to guarantee |\widetilde{\mathrm{Inf}}_i-\mathrm{Inf}_i(f)|<\epsilon for all i with probability at least 1-\delta. In particular, any i observed with y_i=1 in some run is certainly a relevant variable (Inf_i(f)>0), recovering the Floess et al. observation as the special case Inf_i(f)=0.
assumptions: No experiment scope was provided, so the reconstruction targets the core influence-estimation algorithm and uses the tiny instance n=2, f=x_1 x_2 (AND) with a Toffoli oracle.
The oracle model is the standard bit-flip oracle U_f|x\rangle|b\rangle=|x\rangle|b\oplus f(x)\rangle; the abstract does not state it.
The paper's 'dependence degree' is identified with the standard influence Inf_i(f)=Pr_x[f(x)\neq f(x\oplus e_i)], which is the quantity for which the stated identity Pr[y_i=1]=Inf_i(f) holds.

The approximation algorithm is reconstructed as frequency estimation over T independent runs with a Hoeffding/union-bound sample size; the paper's actual estimator, error metric, and query-count statement are unknown.
Register convention: input qubit j stores x_j and yields output bit y_j; x\cdot y is computed modulo 2.
missing_information: The paper's precise definition of 'dependence degree' and the proof of the identity Pr[y_i=1]=Inf_i(f).
The exact form, accuracy guarantee, and query complexity of the paper's approximation algorithm for influence.
